Sources: Fat. 508-510: Laws, political community, and civilization require freedom
Fat. 509: "All political community is constituted upon freedom" (ἐπ᾽ ἐλευθερίᾳ συνέστηκεν)

new:
Premise 1: All human institutions (cities, laws, arts, sciences) presuppose choice (prohairesis)
Premise 2: These institutions exist and function effectively
Conclusion: Therefore choice exists, and not everything is by necessity

Sources: Alexander, De Fato (chapters on deliberation and praise/blame, e.g. the discussion that human beings are by nature deliberative animals, De Fato 11): laws, political community, and the institutions of civilization presuppose that human choices are genuinely "up to us" (eph' hēmin). Alexander argues that political community, laws, the arts and the sciences are all constituted on the assumption of freedom; if determinism abolished what is up to us, these institutions would lose their foundation. [Greek removed: the original node attached two unverifiable Greek phrases to non-existent Bruns page references (Fat. 508-510); De Fato in Bruns runs only to p. 212. Restore verbatim Greek only from a checked edition with correct page/line citation.]

The most comprehensive social argument: determinism doesn't just modify human life but abolishes its foundations. Every institution of civilization assumes that human choices matter and can be influenced. This stakes out the full civilizational cost of accepting determinism.

old: Greek terminology: • κοινὴ αἰτία (koinē aitia) - common cause • ἡ προαίρεσις αἰτία κοινή (hē prohairesis aitia koinē) - choice as common cause • ὁ ἥλιος ἐπὶ τοῦ λοξοῦ κύκλου (ho hēlios epi tou loxou kuklou) - sun on the oblique circle (ecliptic)
new:
Greek terminology: • koinē aitia (common cause) is a genuine technical notion in the ancient causal-classification debate. [The node previously embedded two further Greek phrases — a 'choice as common cause' gloss and a 'sun on the oblique circle' phrase — attributed to Alexander's De Fato without a verifiable locus; both are removed pending a checked edition, since neither is attested in the corpus, in Sharples 1983, or in any catalogued Greek text of De Fato.]

Argument structure: Alexander proposes an alternative causal model to Stoic chain causation: Premise 1: Stoics see causation as linear chains: A→B→C→D Premise 2: But many causal structures involve common causes: A→B, A→C, A→D Premise 3: A single astronomical cause (such as the sun's position on the ecliptic) can be the common cause of several effects (seasons, day length, temperature) Premise 4: Similarly, prohairesis (rational choice) is the common cause of deliberation, action, and outcome Conclusion: Free agents are common causes, not links in deterministic chains Philosophical significance: This reconceptualizes human agency: Agent is not merely one link in causal chain. Agent is source (archē) from which multiple causal paths emanate. This preserves genuine origination while acknowledging causal structure. Scholarly context: The common cause model is presented as Alexander's positive alternative to both Stoic determinism and Epicurean randomness, grounding what modern scholars term libertarian freedom in a coherent causal framework.

These loci are impossible (De Fato in Bruns ends at p. 212) and the phrases are unattested in the corpus, in Sharples 1983, or in any catalogued Greek of De Fato; they are removed pending a checked edition.]

Argument structure:
1. What is truly up to us: assent, choice, impulse, desire, aversion, judgment
2. These constitute our essential being as humans
3. Without these, we would be irrational animals or plants
4. Therefore eph' hēmin is necessary for human existence

Philosophical significance:
Alexander moves from descriptive claim (eph' hēmin exists) to essential claim (eph' hēmin is necessary for humanity). Determinism doesn't just deny a fact but would eliminate the very thing that makes us human. This raises the stakes maximally. [Bruns page references to 'Fat. 498/499/500' removed as fabricated.]
